prompt: What is the key characteristic of a composition reaction?

choices.text: It produces a single substance as its only product.
It starts from a single substance and produces more than one substance.
choices.why: That describes a decomposition reaction, the opposite of a composition reaction.

choices.text: One element takes the place of another element in a compound.
choices.why: That describes a single-replacement reaction, which has two products: a new element and a new compound.

choices.text: It always has exactly two elements as its reactants.
choices.why: The reactants can be compounds, and there can be more than two of them. What matters is that only one substance is produced.

explanation: A composition reaction produces a single substance from multiple reactants. Having just one substance as the product is its key characteristic.

prompt: Which description fits a decomposition reaction?

choices.text: A single reactant forms two or more products.
Two or more reactants form a single product.
choices.why: That is a composition reaction. A decomposition goes the other way, from one substance to several.

choices.text: Any reaction that forms two or more products.
choices.why: Replacement and combustion reactions also form several products. A decomposition must also start from only one reactant.

choices.text: Two compounds exchange parts to form two new compounds.
choices.why: That is a double-replacement reaction. It starts with two reactants, not one.

explanation: A decomposition reaction starts from one substance and produces more than one substance. Both parts matter: one reactant, and more than one product.

prompt: A reaction that produces a single substance from multiple reactants is called a composition reaction. What is another name for it?

choices.text: synthesis reaction
decomposition reaction
choices.why: A decomposition reaction is the opposite: one reactant forms several products.

choices.text: combustion reaction
choices.why: Combustion is a separate classification: a reactant combines with oxygen to produce oxides.

choices.text: replacement reaction
choices.why: In a replacement reaction, an element or ion takes the place of another in a compound. Nothing is replaced when substances simply combine.

explanation: A composition reaction is sometimes also called a combination reaction or a synthesis reaction. All three names describe forming a single product from multiple reactants.

prompt: Which description fits a combustion reaction?

choices.text: A reactant combines with oxygen to produce oxides of the other elements in it.
A compound breaks down and releases oxygen gas.
choices.why: In combustion, O2 is a reactant, not a product. A compound breaking apart to release O2 is a decomposition.

choices.text: Any reaction that produces carbon dioxide and water.
choices.why: Some reactions produce CO2 and H2O without any O2 reacting, such as the decomposition of NaHCO3. Combustion is defined by a reactant combining with oxygen.

choices.text: Two elements combine to form a single compound.
choices.why: That describes a composition reaction. Combustion is defined by a reactant combining with oxygen to produce oxides.

explanation: In a combustion reaction, a reactant combines with oxygen, often from the air, to produce oxides of the other elements. Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen, for example, react with O2 to produce CO2 and H2O.

prompt: A fuel made only of carbon and hydrogen burns to form CO2 and H2O. Which statement explains where these products come from?

choices.text: Each element in the fuel combines with oxygen from O2 to form an oxide of that element.
The fuel already contains CO2 and H2O molecules, which are released when it burns.
choices.why: The fuel is a compound of only carbon and hydrogen, so it contains no oxygen at all. The CO2 and H2O are new substances made in the reaction.

choices.text: The fuel breaks apart on its own, without oxygen, to form CO2 and H2O.
choices.why: The fuel has no oxygen atoms, so the oxygen in CO2 and H2O must come from O2. That's why O2 is a reactant.

choices.text: Oxygen takes the place of the hydrogen in the fuel, as in a single-replacement reaction.
choices.why: Combustion is not a replacement. Every element in the fuel, carbon and hydrogen alike, ends up combined with oxygen.

explanation: Combustion produces oxides of all the other elements in the reactant. The carbon atoms end up in CO2 and the hydrogen atoms end up in H2O, with all the oxygen coming from O2.

prompt: Some fuels contain nitrogen atoms as well as carbon and hydrogen. According to the section, what do the nitrogen atoms become when such a fuel burns?

choices.text: N2
NO2
choices.why: Combustion makes oxides of most elements, but nitrogen is the exception. It is converted to N2, not to a nitrogen-oxygen compound.

choices.text: NH3
choices.why: The hydrogen in the fuel combines with oxygen to form H2O; it doesn't stay with the nitrogen. The nitrogen becomes N2.

choices.text: HNO3
choices.why: Combustion doesn't produce acids. The nitrogen in a fuel ends up as elemental nitrogen, N2.

explanation: If nitrogen is present in a fuel, it is converted to elemental nitrogen, N2, not to a nitrogen-oxygen compound. The other elements still form oxides, such as CO2 and H2O.

prompt: Ethylene glycol, C2H6O2, contains oxygen atoms and can be burned as a fuel. How should the oxygen atoms in its formula be handled when balancing its combustion equation?

choices.text: Count them together with the oxygen from O2 when balancing oxygen.
Ignore them, since in combustion only O2 supplies oxygen.
choices.why: Every atom must be counted. The oxygen atoms in the fuel end up in the CO2 and H2O along with the oxygen from O2.

choices.text: Write them as a separate O2 product on the right side.
choices.why: The fuel's oxygen isn't released as O2; it ends up in the CO2 and H2O products.

choices.text: Change the formula to C2H6 so the fuel contains no oxygen.
choices.why: You can never change a formula to balance an equation. C2H6 is a different substance, ethane.

explanation: Fuels that contain oxygen atoms are balanced the same way, but their oxygen atoms must be counted. Oxygen on the reactant side is the fuel's oxygen plus the oxygen in O2.

prompt: Which equation represents a composition reaction?

choices.text: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2
MgCO3 → MgO + CO2
choices.why: One substance forms two products, so this is a decomposition reaction.

choices.text: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu
choices.why: Iron replaces copper in the compound, so this is a single-replacement reaction with two products.

choices.text: BaCl2 + K2SO4 → BaSO4 + 2KCl
choices.why: Two compounds exchange ions to form two new compounds, so this is a double-replacement reaction.

explanation: In CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2, two reactants form a single substance, which is the mark of a composition reaction. Each of the other equations has more than one product.

prompt: Which equation represents a decomposition reaction?

choices.text: 2Ag2O → 4Ag + O2
Li2O + CO2 → Li2CO3
choices.why: Two reactants form one product, so this is a composition reaction.
This has more than one product, but it has two reactants. A fuel combining with O2 is a combustion reaction.

choices.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
choices.why: This has two products, but also two reactants that exchange ions, so it is a double-replacement reaction.

explanation: In 2Ag2O → 4Ag + O2, a single substance, silver oxide, produces two substances. One reactant and more than one product make it a decomposition reaction.

prompt: Which equation represents a combustion reaction?

choices.text: H2CO3 → H2O + CO2
choices.why: CO2 and H2O form, but no O2 reacts. One substance breaking into two is a decomposition reaction.
O2 is a product here, not a reactant. One substance breaking apart is a decomposition reaction.

choices.text: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2
choices.why: Magnesium replaces hydrogen in HCl, so this is a single-replacement reaction. No O2 is involved.

explanation: In a combustion reaction, a reactant combines with O2 to produce oxides of its other elements. Pentane, C5H12, reacts with O2 to form CO2 and H2O.

prompt: When a car's air bag goes off, sodium azide breaks down and fills the bag with nitrogen gas: 2NaN3 → 2Na + 3N2. How is this reaction classified?

choices.text: Decomposition, because one substance forms more than one product
Composition, because both of the products are elements
choices.why: A composition reaction has a single product. This reaction has two products, Na and N2.

choices.text: Combustion, because it quickly produces a large amount of gas
choices.why: Combustion needs O2 as a reactant and produces oxides. No oxygen is involved here.

choices.text: Single replacement, because an element is one of the products
choices.why: A single replacement also needs an element as a reactant to take another element's place. Here one compound simply breaks apart.

explanation: The only reactant is NaN3, and it produces two substances, Na and N2. One reactant and more than one product is a decomposition reaction.

prompt: Ammonia, water, and carbon dioxide react to form ammonium hydrogen carbonate: NH3 + H2O + CO2 → NH4HCO3. How should this reaction be classified?

choices.text: Composition, because several reactants form a single substance
Not composition, because a composition reaction has exactly two reactants
choices.why: The definition only requires multiple reactants and a single product. Three reactants is fine.

choices.text: Combustion, because CO2 and H2O take part in the reaction
choices.why: CO2 and H2O are reactants here, not products, and no O2 reacts. This is not a combustion reaction.

choices.text: Decomposition, because the product contains four different elements
choices.why: A decomposition starts from a single reactant. The number of elements in a product doesn't decide the type.

explanation: Three substances combine to produce a single substance, NH4HCO3. A single substance as the product is the key characteristic of a composition reaction.

prompt: Hydrogen and chlorine react: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. A student says this can't be a composition reaction because two molecules of HCl are produced. Is the student right?

choices.text: No; only one substance, HCl, is produced, so it is a composition reaction.
Yes; the product of a composition reaction must have a coefficient of 1.
choices.why: The product can have a coefficient other than one. What matters is that there is only one substance as the product.

choices.text: Yes; producing two molecules makes this a decomposition reaction.
choices.why: A decomposition starts from a single reactant. This reaction has two reactants, H2 and Cl2.

choices.text: No; it is a single-replacement reaction, because chlorine replaces hydrogen.
choices.why: Both reactants are elements, so there is no compound for chlorine to replace anything in.

explanation: There may be a coefficient other than one on the product, but if the reaction has only a single substance as its product, it is a composition reaction. Two molecules of HCl are still just one substance.

prompt: A student classifies 2KOH + MgCl2 → Mg(OH)2 + 2KCl as a decomposition reaction because it has more than one product. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: A decomposition starts from one reactant; here two compounds exchange ions, so it is a double replacement.
Nothing; any reaction with more than one product is a decomposition.
choices.why: A decomposition needs a single reactant as well as several products. This reaction has two reactants.

choices.text: It is a composition reaction, because Mg(OH)2 is the only solid formed.
choices.why: KCl is also a product. With two products, it can't be a composition reaction.

choices.text: It is a combustion reaction, because KOH contains oxygen.
choices.why: Combustion needs O2 as a reactant. Oxygen inside a compound doesn't make a reaction a combustion.

explanation: Two compounds react and swap ions to make two new compounds. That fits neither composition nor decomposition; it is a double-replacement reaction.

prompt: Phosphorus pentachloride breaks down when heated: PCl5 → PCl3 + Cl2. When cooled, the products recombine: PCl3 + Cl2 → PCl5. How are these two reactions classified?

choices.text: The first is a decomposition and the second is a composition.
The first is a composition and the second is a decomposition.
choices.why: These are swapped. The first starts from one substance and forms two, which is a decomposition.

choices.text: Both are single-replacement reactions, because Cl2 is an element.
choices.why: Cl2 doesn't replace anything in either reaction. In the second it simply combines with PCl3.

choices.text: Both are decompositions, because both involve PCl5.
choices.why: The type depends on what is reacting and what is formed. In the second reaction, two substances form one, so it is a composition.

explanation: PCl5 → PCl3 + Cl2 has one reactant and two products, so it is a decomposition. The reverse, PCl3 + Cl2 → PCl5, has two reactants and a single product, so it is a composition.

prompt: A student claims that a decomposition reaction always breaks a compound down into its elements. Which equation shows that this claim is wrong?

choices.text: CuCO3 → CuO + CO2
2HgO → 2Hg + O2
choices.why: Both products, Hg and O2, are elements, so this example fits the student's claim instead of disproving it.

choices.text: 2NaCl → 2Na + Cl2
choices.why: Both products, Na and Cl2, are elements, so this example fits the student's claim instead of disproving it.

choices.text: 2AgBr → 2Ag + Br2
choices.why: Both products, Ag and Br2, are elements, so this example fits the student's claim instead of disproving it.

explanation: A decomposition only needs one reactant and more than one product; the products can be compounds. CuCO3 decomposes into two compounds, CuO and CO2.

prompt: How many of these five equations represent composition reactions? 2K + Br2 → 2KBr; Cu(OH)2 → CuO + H2O; Zn + CuCl2 → ZnCl2 + Cu; SO3 + H2O → H2SO4; 2AgNO3 + CaCl2 → 2AgCl + Ca(NO3)2
explanation: Only 2K + Br2 → 2KBr and SO3 + H2O → H2SO4 produce a single substance. The others are a decomposition, a single replacement, and a double replacement.

prompt: How many of these five equations represent combustion reactions? 2C3H7OH + 9O2 → 6CO2 + 8H2O; Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2; 2KNO3 → 2KNO2 + O2; C12H22O11 + 12O2 → 12CO2 + 11H2O; C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2
explanation: Only the reactions of C3H7OH and C12H22O11 with O2 are combustions, producing CO2 and H2O. The other three produce CO2, H2O, or O2, but no reactant combines with O2.

prompt: A fuel burns in oxygen, and the only products are CO2 and H2O. Based on the section, which elements could the fuel contain?

choices.text: Carbon and hydrogen, and possibly oxygen
Carbon and hydrogen only, because fuels can't contain oxygen
choices.why: Fuels can contain oxygen, as ethanol does. The fuel's oxygen also ends up in CO2 and H2O, so it wouldn't show up as a separate product.

choices.text: Carbon, hydrogen, and sulfur
choices.why: Combustion produces oxides of all the other elements, so sulfur would form a sulfur oxide as another product.

choices.text: Carbon and oxygen only
choices.why: O2 contains no hydrogen, so the hydrogen in the H2O must have come from the fuel.

explanation: Combustion produces oxides of the elements in the fuel: carbon gives CO2 and hydrogen gives H2O. Oxygen in the fuel ends up in those same products, so the fuel may or may not contain oxygen.

prompt: Hydrazine, N2H4, is burned as a rocket fuel. Which balanced equation correctly represents its combustion?

choices.text: N2H4 + O2 → N2 + 2H2O

choices.why: The atoms balance, but nitrogen in a fuel is converted to N2, not to a nitrogen-oxygen compound.

choices.text: N2H4 + O2 → N2 + H2O
choices.why: The products are right, but the equation isn't balanced: there are 4 H atoms on the left and only 2 on the right.
This is balanced, but nothing combines with oxygen. One substance breaking apart is a decomposition, not a combustion.

explanation: The nitrogen becomes N2 and the hydrogen combines with oxygen to form H2O. Four H atoms need 2H2O, which holds 2 O atoms, supplied by one O2: N2H4 + O2 → N2 + 2H2O.

prompt: A student balances the combustion of glucose, C6H12O6, as C6H12O6 + 9O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O. What went wrong?

choices.text: The six oxygen atoms in glucose weren't counted; the coefficient of O2 should be 6.
Nothing; the equation is balanced as written.
choices.why: Count the oxygen: 6 + 18 = 24 atoms on the left, but only 12 + 6 = 18 on the right.

choices.text: H2O should have a coefficient of 12 to match the 12 hydrogen atoms.
choices.why: Each H2O molecule has two hydrogen atoms, so 6H2O already holds all 12.

choices.text: Glucose already contains oxygen, so O2 shouldn't be a reactant.
choices.why: Combustion is a reaction with O2. Glucose doesn't contain nearly enough oxygen to form 6CO2 and 6H2O by itself.

explanation: The products hold 6 × 2 + 6 = 18 oxygen atoms. Glucose supplies 6 of them, so O2 must supply 12, which is 6O2: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O.

prompt: A student writes the combustion of ethylene as C2H4 + 2O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2. What should the student fix?

choices.text: H2 should be H2O; the correct equation is C2H4 + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2O.
Nothing; the atoms balance, so the equation is correct.
choices.why: Balanced atoms aren't enough. In combustion, hydrogen combines with oxygen to form H2O; it isn't released as H2.

choices.text: H2 should be H2O; the correct equation is C2H4 + 2O2 → 2CO2 + 2H2O.
choices.why: The products are right, but there are now 6 oxygen atoms on the right and only 4 on the left. It needs 3O2.

choices.text: CO2 should be CO; the correct equation is C2H4 + O2 → 2CO + 2H2.
choices.why: This adds a second mistake: carbon in a fuel like this ends up as CO2, and the hydrogen still has to form H2O.

explanation: Combustion produces oxides of all the other elements, so the hydrogen must end up in H2O. Then the right side has 2 × 2 + 2 = 6 oxygen atoms, which takes 3O2.

prompt: Ethane, C2H6, burns in oxygen. Write its combustion equation and balance it using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of O2?
explanation: The products are CO2 and H2O: 2C2H6 + 7O2 → 4CO2 + 6H2O. With one C2H6, O2 would need a coefficient of 3.5, so every coefficient is doubled to avoid a fraction.

prompt: Welders burn acetylene, C2H2, in oxygen. Write its combustion equation and balance it using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of CO2?
explanation: C2H2 + O2 → CO2 + H2O balances as 2C2H2 + 5O2 → 4CO2 + 2H2O. With one C2H2, the right side holds 5 oxygen atoms, so every coefficient is doubled to avoid 2.5O2.

prompt: Butane, C4H10, is the fuel in disposable lighters. Write its combustion equation and balance it using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the sum of all the coefficients, counting any coefficient of 1?
explanation: The balanced equation is 2C4H10 + 13O2 → 8CO2 + 10H2O, so the sum is 2 + 13 + 8 + 10 = 33. With one C4H10, O2 would need 6.5, so every coefficient is doubled.

prompt: Methanol, CH3OH, is burned as a racing fuel. Write its combustion equation and balance it using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of O2?
explanation: The balanced equation is 2CH3OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 4H2O. The products hold 8 oxygen atoms; the two methanol molecules supply 2 of them, so O2 supplies 6, which is 3O2.

prompt: Carbon disulfide, CS2, burns in oxygen to form oxides of both of its elements: carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, SO2. Balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of O2?
explanation: CS2 + O2 → CO2 + SO2 balances as CS2 + 3O2 → CO2 + 2SO2. The two sulfur atoms need 2SO2, so the right side has 2 + 4 = 6 oxygen atoms, which takes 3O2.

prompt: Gasoline can be approximated as octane, C8H18. Its balanced combustion equation is 2C8H18 + 25O2 → 16CO2 + 18H2O. How many oxygen atoms appear on each side of the equation?
explanation: On the left, 25O2 holds 25 × 2 = 50 oxygen atoms. On the right, 16CO2 holds 32 and 18H2O holds 18, for 50, so oxygen is balanced.

prompt: Aluminum metal and iodine, I2, combine in a composition reaction to form aluminum iodide. Write the equation and balance it using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of I2?
explanation: Aluminum forms Al^3+ and iodine forms I−, so the single product is AlI3. Balancing Al + I2 → AlI3 gives 2Al + 3I2 → 2AlI3.

prompt: Nitrogen triiodide, NI3, is so unstable that a light touch makes it decompose into nitrogen gas, N2, and iodine, I2. Balance the equation using the smallest whole-number coefficients. What is the coefficient of NI3?
explanation: NI3 → N2 + I2 balances as 2NI3 → N2 + 3I2. Two NI3 provide the two nitrogen atoms in N2 and six iodine atoms for 3I2.
